Leishmaniasis

A single uncontrolled pilot found complete or partial responses in early-grade lesions but no responses in advanced-grade lesions.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

A single uncontrolled pilot found complete or partial responses in early-grade lesions but no responses in advanced-grade lesions.

Summary of the Evidence

One human single-arm pilot studied 53 people with cutaneous leishmaniasis and 123 lesions. Lesions were nested within patients, so 123 is not the number of independent participants. The report separated early-grade lesions from advanced disease. No randomized or controlled PBM study, animal experiment, or separate in-vitro study for cutaneous leishmaniasis was identified in the relevant database category.

Human and clinical evidence

The pilot used laser treatment four times over four weeks and followed participants for ten months. At follow-up, complete response was reported in 91% of patients with low-grade disease and partial response in the remaining 9%. No response was reported among patients with high-grade lesions. Because everyone received PBM and lesion counts were clustered within patients, the study cannot determine how much of the response was caused by treatment or compare PBM with standard antileishmanial care (Khan et al. 2020).

Animal evidence

No animal study directly evaluating PBM for cutaneous leishmaniasis was identified.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No separate parasite, cell-culture, or tissue experiment directly testing PBM for this indication was identified in the mapped evidence.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The investigators applied a 635-nm red visible laser at 300 mW and 75 J/cm² to the lesions, with four weekly sessions. The study did not compare wavelengths, fluences, or schedules. These parameters therefore describe one pilot protocol and do not establish an optimal dose. The marked difference between early- and advanced-grade results also limits generalization across lesion severity.

Interpretation

The pilot reported complete or partial response for early-grade lesions and no response for advanced-grade disease at ten months. This is a clinically notable pattern within one uncontrolled sample, not a comparative estimate of treatment effect. A controlled trial should analyze patients as the independent units, standardize disease grading, and report lesion healing and parasitological outcomes alongside usual care.

Evidence strength in source summaryVery low for early-stage cutaneous lesion response
Publications and records1 unique publication

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

The pilot reported complete or partial responses for early-grade lesions, but its 53 patients received treatment without a comparator and 123 lesions were clustered within those patients. Advanced-grade lesions did not respond. A controlled study with patient-level allocation, standardized lesion grading, and comparison against usual antileishmanial care is needed before estimating a causal effect.

  • No animal or in-vitro studies identified
